html:
A month-long visit to India by the American civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. in February and March 1959, to learn about the nonviolent methods of Mahatma Gandhi.

King had used Gandhian ideas in the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, which made him famous. He knew Gandhi's ideas from reading and from Black American thinkers who had visited India before. Gandhi had been dead for over a decade, but King wanted to see the country where satyagraha, mass nonviolent resistance, had helped end British rule. He travelled with his wife Coretta Scott King, met Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, spoke with Gandhi's followers and visited the places of the Salt March. On arrival he said: "To other countries I may go as a tourist, but to India I come as a pilgrim."

He came home more committed than ever to nonviolence, not just as a tactic but as a way of life. The campaigns that followed helped win the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The idea had travelled a long way: Gandhi first developed it in South Africa.
sum: A month-long visit to India by the American civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. in February and March 1959, to learn about the nonviolent methods of Mahatma Gandhi.
